Case Study

Medication Recommender Cost Analysis

Giving Providers the Cost Data They Were Missing at the Moment That Matters

Role
Senior UX/UI Designer
Type
Professional Work
Company
Optum Technology
Tools
Figma · UserZoom · Jira

The Patient Cost popover, shown in context inside the Epic EHR medication ordering workflow

Overview

Prescribing Blind

Every medication recommendation carries a hidden variable: what it will actually cost the patient. Without real-time cost data embedded in their workflow, providers were prescribing medications they had no way to know patients could afford. This project was about closing that gap without disrupting the clinical encounter.

Who We Built This For

Primary care and specialty providers prescribing in real time with patients in the room. They had seconds, not minutes, to weigh efficacy against affordability. Cost data had to arrive at exactly the right moment and be instantly legible.

Problem Statement

The Design Question

How might we make patient cost data feel like a natural part of the clinical decision, not an interruption to it?

Objectives & Goals

01

Embed estimated patient cost directly in the CDS medication table, with zero added steps

02

Make formulary status and cost scannable at a glance, not a task to complete

03

Validate design decisions through moderated research with real providers, not assumptions

04

Deliver a final design that providers trust enough to act on during a live patient visit

Constraints

Designing Inside a Live Workflow

Cost and formulary data had to surface inside an already dense CDS table during a live patient visit, with no room for new screens. The design was also bound by the limits of the underlying formulary API and validated against a tight research window of five variants tested with fifteen providers.

Process

Research-Led, Iteration-Driven

We did not design in a vacuum. Fifteen providers sat through moderated sessions where we put competing designs in front of them and asked them to think aloud. Every design decision is traceable to something a real participant said or did. No assumption survived without evidence.

01
Discover
  • Stakeholder interviews
  • Clinical workflow mapping
  • EHR constraint review
02
Define
  • Component prioritization
  • Test artifact design
  • Research protocol
03
Test
  • 15 moderated sessions
  • Preference testing
  • Think-aloud protocol
04

  • Alert pattern exploration
  • Final design delivery

Team: 1 Product Owner · 1 UX Researcher · 2 UX/UI Designers · Engineering

Research

Putting 5 Variants in Front of Real Providers

We tested one design question at a time: which link style felt most clickable, which column layout was most readable, which popover fields were actually useful. Each round tightened the design space until the right pattern became undeniable.

The initial test artifact: five GLP-1 RA medications with a highlighted Patient Cost column, presented to 15 providers to evaluate link style preferences

Patient Cost Controls preference results: the plain link style won decisively because providers immediately understood what clicking it would do

Patient Cost Breakdown findings: Estimated Patient Cost and Prior Authorization earned high trust; Alerts, vague type labels, and Step Therapy language were flagged as confusing or removable

Research

How Much to Show in the Table?

The central tension: how much belongs in the table versus behind a click? Too little and the column feels useless. Too much and providers stop reading it. We built four variants across the full density spectrum and let the data decide.

Four pricing column variants tested side-by-side: from cost-only minimal display to full formulary status with copay tier breakdowns

Option B won 11 to 15: color-coded formulary status, icons paired with text, single-column format. Providers asked for more descriptive titles and tier-level color differentiation

Research

What Providers Actually Used

We dissected the popover field by field. Not every piece of data providers think they want is data they actually act on. This phase separated the essential from the optional, and the precise from the misleading.

Patient Cost tab findings: Description, Prior Authorization, and Estimated Patient Cost were rated critical. 7 of 15 providers said they would skip alerts entirely, forcing a rethink of alert prominence

Plan Level Details: pharmacy types and days supply were most valued. Copay ranges and Tier numbering ("Tier 1 of 3") confused most participants

Coverage Factors: Step Therapy and Prior Authorization earned top priority. Coverage messages were called vague, and Gender Restriction was considered unnecessary by most

Medication Type: 11 of 15 misread the label as referring to drug class. Splitting it into "Brand name or generic" and "Prescription or over-the-counter" resolved the confusion for 12 of 15 participants

Design

From Debate to Decision

Alerts nearly broke the design. Too prominent and providers tuned them out. Too buried and they became a liability. We explored three distinct column treatments to find the balance between urgency and noise, then consolidated everything learned into a single, resolved system.

Three alert column treatments tested: Comfy, Condensed, and Labeled. Each explored a different answer to how much visual weight an alert should carry inside a clinical table

Final design: the Patient Cost Breakdown popover resolved into three clear sections (Copay Factors, Coverage Factors, Payer-Recommended Alternatives), paired with a clean Medication Cost column in the CDS table

Edge case coverage: Copay amount scenarios, Step Therapy requirements, and the "Pharmacy is disabled" state, all accounted for in the final design system

Final Patient Cost tab system: complete view of the Patient Cost and Plan Level Details tabs, all coverage factor states, payer-recommended alternatives, and every Copay and Step Therapy scenario designed and documented

Trade-offs

Alternatives Considered

01

A distinct visual treatment, or a familiar one?

We considered a visually distinct treatment for cost links using icons and color coded badges, but chose the plain, familiar link style instead. Research showed that visual novelty created hesitation at exactly the moment clinical confidence mattered most.

02

Prominent alerts, or collapsed ones?

We considered surfacing alerts prominently by default, but chose to deprioritize and collapse them instead. Seven of fifteen providers said they would skip alerts entirely, so visibility was working against us.

03

Patch the label, or rewrite it?

We considered patching the confusing "Medication Type" label with added help text, but chose to split it into two plain language fields instead. That cost some table width but recovered trust across the entire panel.

Outcomes

The Numbers Behind the Design

15
Providers tested the product across multiple research rounds, each focused on a different design component
11/15
Providers aligned on Option B, turning the column decision from a design preference into a research finding
4
Distinct UI components rebuilt from the ground up based on what providers actually said in sessions

Conclusions

What Changed How We Designed

01

Providers trust what they already understand

The standard link style won because it matched a mental model providers already had. Visually richer alternatives introduced just enough unfamiliarity to create hesitation at the exact moment clinical confidence mattered most.

02

If everything is urgent, nothing is

7 of 15 providers said they would skip alerts entirely. That finding reshaped the entire information hierarchy: alerts were deprioritized in the table and collapsed by default in the popover, visible only to providers who actively chose to look.

03

Ambiguous labels undermined the whole panel

When a single label confused providers, it cast doubt on the entire panel. Rewriting "Medication Type" into two plain-language fields did not just fix a label; it recovered trust in everything around it.

Future Iterations

Unfinished Business

Alert Design

Test a progressive disclosure pattern where alerts are collapsed by default and expand on demand. The goal: find out whether providers catch critical safety information more reliably when they choose to look, versus when it competes for attention automatically.

Patient View

Explore a shareable patient-facing cost summary providers can display or print during the visit. Reducing the verbal explanation burden while giving patients something concrete to reference could close the gap between recommendation and follow-through.

Pharmacy Data

Evaluate surfacing preferred pharmacy availability alongside the cost estimate. An accurate cost figure loses value if the patient cannot fill it at a convenient location. Participants raised this in sessions and it is worth testing at scale.

Longitudinal

Measure whether surfacing cost data at the point of care actually shifts prescribing behavior. The design hypothesis is that visibility drives action. Tracking prescription choices before and after adoption would prove or challenge that assumption.
